name: DRV8662RGPT
title: DRV8662: piezo haptic driver with built-in 105 V boost converter
summary: A single-chip driver for piezo haptic actuators. From a 3.3 V to 5.5 V battery it boosts, with one external inductor and its own switch and diode, to an adjustable rail of 15 V to 105 V, and a fully differential amplifier on that rail swings the piezo up to 200 VPP. Two pins choose one of four gains (28.8 to 40.7 dB) for a differential or single-ended analog input; one resistor sets the boost current limit and two set the boost voltage. It starts in 1.5 ms from EN, protects itself thermally, and comes in a 4 mm × 4 mm 20-pin VQFN.
key_figures: 100 nF at 200 VPP; 680 nF at 50 VPP
5 kHz at 40.7 dB, 20 kHz at 28.8 dB

notes: All four are the same die in the same 20-pin 4 mm × 4 mm VQFN; they differ only in reel size (R: 3000 a reel, T: 250 a reel) and in the listed lead finish.

circuits.title: Piezo drive from a differential DAC
circuits.description: The battery feeds VDD and one end of L1; the other end of L1 goes to SW, and the internal switch and diode lift VBST, held up by C2. PVDD takes its supply from VBST. R1 and R2 divide VBST down to FB and so set the boost voltage; R3 on REXT sets the switch current limit. C3 holds the charge pump output on VPUMP. A DAC drives IN+ and IN- differentially through the 1 µF coupling capacitors C4 and C5, and the bridge outputs OUT+ and OUT- drive the two terminals of the piezo. EN, GAIN1 and GAIN0 come from the system's digital control. The design example uses a 1.8 V peak sine at the inputs, a 20 V to 105 V boost rail and an output of twice the boost voltage peak to peak.

circuits.title: Piezo drive from a filtered single-ended PWM signal
circuits.description: The power side is the same as the DAC example: L1 and the internal switch boost VBAT to VBST on C2, PVDD tied to VBST, R1 and R2 setting the boost voltage at FB, R3 setting the current limit, C3 on VPUMP. The processor's PWM pin drives a first-order low-pass of R4 and C6 to ground, whose output reaches IN+ through C4. IN- is returned to ground through C5, so the input is single-ended. The outputs drive the piezo between OUT+ and OUT-. The design example uses a 1.8 V peak PWM signal.

operation.text: From a 3.3 V to 5.5 V supply, an on-chip boost converter (power switch and diode both inside) makes a rail of up to 105 V that powers a fully differential high-voltage amplifier. The amplifier drives a capacitive load such as a piezo with up to 200 VPP across it. One external inductor is needed and no transformer. A thermal shutdown block and a charge pump for internal gate drive are also on chip.

At 300 Hz the largest loads are 100 nF for 200 VPP, 150 nF for 150 VPP, 330 nF for 100 VPP and 680 nF for 50 VPP. At 500 Hz and 200 VPP it drives up to 50 nF. Lowering the boost voltage, or keeping the signal at lower frequencies, allows more capacitance.
A rising edge on EN starts the boost supply, pre-charges the input capacitors and then turns on the amplifier; the whole start-up takes 1.5 ms typical. With EN low the part draws 13 µA typical.

GAIN1 and GAIN0 select 28.8, 34.8, 38.4 or 40.7 dB. Fed 1.8 V peak on one input, they give about 50, 100, 150 and 200 VPP at the outputs without clipping. The input may be differential or single-ended; input impedance is 100 kΩ at every gain.
A divider from VBST to FB sets the boost output, at most 105 V. It is set above the highest output peak expected; a lower boost voltage gives better efficiency when the signal amplitude is low.

A resistor from REXT to ground sets the peak current through the boost switch and inductor. Choose a limit below the inductor's saturation current, or the inductor and the part can both be damaged. If the limit or the inductor's saturation current is too low, the boost cannot hold VBST under heavy load; the rail sags and the output waveform can distort. The boost never draws more supply current than this limit.
An internal charge pump supplies gate drive inside the chip and brings it out on VPUMP, which needs a 0.1 µF X5R or X7R capacitor rated 10 V or more to GND.

Above its temperature threshold an internal sensor shuts down the amplifier and the boost converter together. Once the die cools below the threshold the part restarts by itself as long as EN is still high. The part is meant for short bursts, not continuous operation. Running the part into thermal shutdown is to be avoided.

1. Start the PWM at 50 % duty into the input filter so source and filter settle; EN goes high together with it, or one processor cycle later. 2. Wait 2 ms for the part to be fully on and settled. 3. Play the waveform, finishing at 50 % duty so the differential output returns to 0 V. 4. Pull EN low, then switch the PWM source off. Skipping the sequence can cause unwanted haptic events or sounds.

1. Set the DAC to mid-scale so source and input capacitors settle; EN goes high together with it, or one processor cycle later. 2. Wait 2 ms. 3. Play the waveform, ending at the mid-scale code so the differential output returns to 0 V. 4. Pull EN low, then switch the DAC off.

The lowest gain is set for 50 VPP from a 30 V boost. The boost may go as low as 15 V for better efficiency. Below 30 V, use a 0.22 µF boost capacitor rated 50 V to keep boost ripple acceptable, and scale the input to avoid clipping: with VBST = 25 V for 40 VPP, full-scale single-ended PWM input falls to 1.44 V, so a divider may be wanted on a 1.8 V PWM output.

Recommended inductance is 3.3 µH to 22 µH. A larger inductance makes the boost switch more slowly with less switching loss, but larger parts tend to have higher ESR and more conduction loss. Within one inductor series the smaller values usually saturate at higher current, so they are better when the most boost output current is wanted. The DRV8662EVM user's guide (SLOU319) lists inductors.
For the driver the piezo's voltage rating and capacitance are what count. 200 VPP is the highest swing; at 500 Hz the part is set up for up to 50 nF at that swing.
The capacitor on VBST must be rated for at least the boost voltage. For 105 V a 100 nF X5R or X7R part rated 250 V is recommended, keeping at least 50 nF of working capacitance.

A DAC source with good anti-image filtering may need no filter, depending on its out-of-band content. A PWM source needs at least a first-order RC low-pass, and a PWM sample rate above 30 kHz keeps the ripple off the piezo where it would waste power. Haptic content is below 500 Hz, so the filter must attenuate above that. First-order filters, single-ended or differential, suit sample rates of 20 kHz and higher and settle quickly with few parts; at lower rates such as 8 kHz a second-order filter gives the sharper cutoff needed for quiet operation. The filter should cut the PWM carrier by 40 dB or more. The DRV8662EVM ships with a differential filter of second order.

Supply range is 3.3 V to 5.5 V. Put a 0.1 µF low-ESR X5R or X7R capacitor rated 10 V or more near VDD, and a 0.1 µF X5R or X7R capacitor rated 10 V or more from VPUMP to GND. The charge pump is not to supply any other device.
Total haptic system latency below 30 ms goes unnoticed by the user; the 1.5 ms start-up is a small part of that.

Solder the exposed pad to a ground-connected board pad, stitched by thermal vias to inner or back ground planes; tying it to top-layer ground near the package corners also helps. Keep R1 and R2 as close to FB as possible, and route the FB trace away from SW.
